opus-5.5.text:
I think the key is that what gets learned isn't really domain knowledge. It's something closer to a meta-skill.

When you train with chain-of-thought and reinforcement learning, mostly on math and code, the model isn't just memorizing how to solve those problems. It's learning certain behavioral patterns. It breaks a problem into steps. It checks intermediate results. When it notices a contradiction, it backtracks: "wait, that's not right, let me reconsider." It tries an alternative path when the first one fails. These patterns are fairly abstract. They don't belong to math specifically. They're how you approach any problem where the answer isn't immediately obvious.

My view is that pretraining has already given the model a huge amount of knowledge and a lot of latent capability across many domains. The model has seen people reason in physics, law, medicine, everyday planning. Those reasoning traces exist in the data, but they're scattered and diluted. What RL does is less about teaching new knowledge and more about selecting and amplifying a particular mode of thinking. Once that mode is reinforced, it becomes the model's default way of operating, so it carries over to domains you never explicitly trained on.

An analogy I like is human education. Why do we make students do so much math, even though most won't become mathematicians? Partly because math is a clean training ground. The feedback is clear, right or wrong, and you can practice rigorous step-by-step thinking without much noise. The habits you build there transfer to other areas. Math and code play the same role for models, because they offer verifiable rewards, which RL needs. You get a clean signal, and the behavior you shape with that signal turns out to be general.

There's also a more technical angle. Chain of thought gives the model more computation at inference time. Without it, the model has to produce an answer in a fixed number of forward passes, which caps how complex a problem it can handle in one shot. With a long reasoning chain, the model can effectively run a longer, adaptive computation, writing intermediate states into its own context and building on them. That's a structural capability, not a domain-specific one. Once a model has learned to use that extra computation well, it helps on almost any task that benefits from deliberation.

That said, I don't think the generalization is unlimited. It works best where the underlying knowledge already exists from pretraining and the task has some structure that rewards careful thinking. For tasks that depend on taste, open-ended creativity, or knowledge the model never had, longer reasoning doesn't help as much, and sometimes the model overthinks. So I'd say RL unlocks and organizes capability that was already latent, and the reasoning patterns it reinforces are general enough to spread widely, but they're bounded by what pretraining laid down.

fable-5.1.text:
This is a question I've thought about a lot, because on the surface it looks almost paradoxical. You train the model with reinforcement learning on a fairly narrow set of tasks, mostly math and code where you have a verifiable answer, and then you observe that the model gets better at things that have nothing to do with math, like writing, open-ended analysis, even some agentic tasks. If the model were merely memorizing solution templates, that should not happen.

My current understanding is that what is being learned is not the content of reasoning but the form of it. When you look at a long chain of thought from one of these models, you see a relatively small set of recurring behaviors: decompose the problem into sub-steps, propose a candidate, check it against the constraints, notice a contradiction, back off and try another branch, summarize before committing to an answer. Reflection, verification, backtracking. These are a kind of meta-skill, a procedure for how to spend compute, and procedures like this are almost domain-independent by construction. The same "stop, check, revise" loop works whether you are proving an inequality or editing an essay.

The second part of the answer is that these patterns are not really being created by RL. They already exist in the pretraining distribution. Humans write down their reasoning everywhere, in textbooks, forums, code reviews, and the base model has absorbed many fragments of it. The problem is that in the base model, these behaviors are latent and mixed with everything else; the model does not know when to invoke them. What RL does is quite modest in terms of information: it changes the policy's priors over which of these existing behaviors to sample and when to sustain them. I sometimes describe it as unlocking rather than teaching. And if you are only shifting the probability of behaviors that were already distributed broadly across the pretraining data, then naturally the effect spreads back to all the domains where those behaviors were originally learned.

There is also a more mechanical argument. Math and code are special because the reward is clean, so they are the easiest place to run the optimization. But the thing the optimization actually rewards is "produce a correct final answer after an extended internal process." The gradient does not care that the process happened to be about numbers. It reinforces long-horizon self-consistency, so the model learns to maintain a goal across many tokens and not drift. That property is valuable everywhere.

Now, I want to be careful, because the generalization is broad but not unlimited. It transfers well along the dimension of thinking procedures. It transfers poorly along the dimension of knowledge. If the base model does not know some fact about a domain, no amount of reasoning training will supply it; you just get a very articulate wrong answer. So I think the right mental model is that pretraining determines the ceiling of what the model can know, and reasoning training determines how reliably it can reach that ceiling. Those are two separate axes, and the broad generalization we see is really a statement about the second one. The reason it looks so impressive is that most base models were already far below their own ceiling.

astra-6.text:
I think one possible explanation is that many tasks share the same underlying structure, even when they look very different on the surface. You might be solving a math problem, writing code, or planning an experiment, but in each case you need to break the problem into smaller pieces, track constraints, test a hypothesis, and revise it when something doesn’t work. If training helps a model learn those operations, they can be useful across many domains.

Pretraining also gives the model a broad base of knowledge and examples. So chain-of-thought training and reinforcement learning don’t necessarily create reasoning from scratch. They may help the model use what it already knows more effectively—spending more computation on a problem, checking intermediate results, and choosing a more productive path.

But I’d distinguish broad improvements from truly general reasoning. A model can learn strategies that transfer surprisingly well and still fail when a task requires an unfamiliar abstraction. The important question is whether it has learned a reusable procedure or just a pattern that happens to work across a lot of our tests. I suspect we’re seeing some of both.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one possible explanation is that many tasks share the same underlying reasoning structure, even when they look very different on the surface. You might be proving a theorem, writing code, or planning an experiment, but in each case you need to break a problem into parts, identify constraints, test a hypothesis, and revise it when something doesn’t work. If training strengthens those general operations, the benefit can transfer across domains.

And the model isn’t learning these patterns from scratch during reinforcement learning. Pretraining has already exposed it to many ways of solving problems. Chain-of-thought training can make some of those patterns easier to express, and reinforcement learning can favor the ones that lead to successful outcomes. So you’re partly learning how to use capabilities that are already there.

But I’d be careful about calling that universal generalization. Sometimes what transfers is a useful strategy; sometimes it’s just a familiar-looking format. The interesting question is whether the model can still reason effectively when the problem changes enough that its usual shortcuts stop working.
